Name: refusal_certainty_bandwidth
Title: How Sure Is the Refusal? Reading Latent Decision-Certainty to Separate Confident Safety From Brittle Guesswork and Preempt Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Beyond the direction of an LLM's refuse/comply decision, the residual stream encodes the model's internal *certainty* about that decision as a distinct, low-dimensional signal. We hypothesize that (a) genuine harmful and genuine benign prompts sit far from the decision boundary (high certainty), while jailbroken and borderline prompts occupy a low-certainty band, and (b) reading this certainty axis flags brittle safety decisions before the output is produced far better than output-token log-probs, enabling selective escalation only on the small set of low-certainty inputs.
Related Work: Refusal-direction work (Arditi et al.; Pan et al. ICML 2025; Zhao et al. NeurIPS 2025) extracts the *direction* of the refuse/comply decision but treats each prompt as simply on one side of a boundary and ignores how confidently it sits there. Calibration/uncertainty literature (semantic entropy, Kuhn et al. 2023; verbalized confidence) reads output-distribution or self-report signals, not the geometry of the safety decision itself. Jailbreak detectors (perplexity filters, Llama-Guard, gradient-based) use surface/output features. Our distinction: we introduce a *latent decision-certainty* signal for the safety decision specifically—operationalized as distance/margin to the refusal decision boundary and the local curvature/instability of the refusal projection under small activation perturbations—and show that jailbreaks characteristically live in a low-certainty band even when they succeed in flipping the sign, giving a mechanism-grounded, single-pass triage signal orthogonal to prior boundary-sign readouts.
Abstract: Mechanistic work has localized LLM refusal to a low-dimensional direction and reads the sign of a prompt's projection to predict refuse-vs-comply. But sign alone discards a crucial quantity: how confidently the model has made that decision. We propose that the residual stream encodes a distinct latent decision-certainty signal for the safety decision, and that this certainty—not the sign—is what jailbreaks and borderline prompts characteristically degrade. We operationalize decision-certainty two ways: the signed margin to the refusal decision boundary, and the local instability of the refusal projection under small, semantically-neutral activation perturbations (a cheap curvature estimate). Across open-weight chat models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B), we show that clearly harmful and clearly benign prompts occupy high-certainty regions, while jailbroken prompts (GCG, roleplay/DAN, translation, prefix-injection) and genuinely borderline prompts (XSTest, OR-Bench) cluster in a low-certainty band—even when a jailbreak succeeds in flipping the model to comply. This yields a single-forward-pass triage monitor: high-certainty comply/refuse decisions are trusted, and only low-certainty inputs are escalated to expensive checks or conservative defaults. We show this certainty band predicts both jailbreak success and over-refusal risk better than output log-prob confidence, perplexity filters, and self-reported confidence, at far lower cost than always-on guardrails, and that certainty-gated intervention reduces attack success and over-refusal simultaneously by acting only where the model is unsure. Our work adds a missing scalar—confidence—to the geometry of LLM safety decisions.
Experiments: 1) Direction and margin extraction: on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, extract the refusal direction via difference-in-means (harmful vs benign) at the best layer/last prompt token; define signed margin as the projection distance to the fitted decision threshold (calibrated on a held-out mixed set). 2) Curvature/instability certainty: estimate local decision stability by adding K small isotropic (and semantically-neutral paraphrase-induced) perturbations to the residual activation and measuring variance / sign-flip rate of the refusal projection; combine margin + instability into a certainty score. 3) Certainty landscape: on harmful (AdvBench/HarmBench/StrongREJECT), benign (Alpaca), borderline (XSTest, OR-Bench), and jailbroken variants (GCG, roleplay/DAN, low-resource translation, prefix-injection), plot certainty distributions. Test hypothesis: clear-harmful and clear-benign are high-certainty; jailbreaks and borderline are low-certainty; crucially, *successful* jailbreaks that flip to comply still show low certainty relative to genuine benign comply. 4) Triage monitor: use the certainty score to flag low-certainty inputs; compare jailbreak-detection AUROC, over-refusal prediction, TPR@1%FPR against (i) output-token log-prob / entropy confidence, (ii) semantic entropy over sampled completions, (iii) verbalized self-confidence, (iv) perplexity input filter, (v) Llama-Guard. Report the fraction of inputs that are high-certainty (cheaply trusted) vs escalated. 5) Certainty-gated intervention: for low-certainty inputs only, apply a conservative default (refusal steering or an expensive secondary check); measure joint reduction in attack success rate (harmful sets) AND over-refusal rate (XSTest/OR-Bench), plus utility on MMLU/MT-Bench, versus always-on steering and no defense. 6) Cross-model / leave-one-attack-out generalization of the certainty score and monitor. Metrics: AUROC, TPR@1%FPR, escalation fraction, ASR reduction, over-refusal rate, utility delta, per-attack transfer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The certainty signal may be largely redundant with output-distribution entropy; we mitigate by directly comparing and reporting the marginal gain, and by measuring cases where they disagree. 2) Some strong jailbreaks may produce genuinely high-certainty (confidently wrong) comply decisions, limiting coverage—this failure mode is itself informative and reported per attack family. 3) The curvature/instability estimate adds K forward-ish passes; we report cost and test a cheap single-pass margin-only variant. 4) Isotropic activation perturbations may not correspond to semantically meaningful input changes; we cross-check with paraphrase-induced perturbations. 5) Threshold calibration may not transfer across models; we recalibrate per model and report sensitivity. 6) Results are on mid-size open-weight models; frontier transfer is untested, though the certainty-geometry framing is model-agnostic.
